_comment: The Log. Dated record of what was worked on. Back-catalogue reconstructed on 2026-08-31 from a file inventory of 1,450 documents, so the dates are file dates rather than memory. Newest first. No cadence: entries appear when work happens.

entries.title: The site had no typeface, and that was most of the problem
entries.body:
Georgia, a system sans stack, and Consolas. Three fallbacks and nothing chosen. That is most of why the site read as amateur, and it took somebody saying so plainly before anyone looked.

Three other causes, all of them the same kind of mistake. Three accent colours at full chroma, every one worn as a bordered pill, which is dashboard vocabulary rather than the vocabulary of a record. Radial glow gradients sitting behind the body, the single clearest tell of a 2015 dark theme. And a gold that was really yellow with the saturation raised, where metal sits lower in chroma and leans toward brass.

What replaced it is a ruled sheet. Libre Caslon Text for everything that gets read, IBM Plex Mono for every date, label and figure. Gilt draws a hairline and never fills a shape. Emerald carries structure. The lightning blue is held back for links alone, so it means something on the rare occasion it appears. Nothing is a chip. A hundred and nineteen lines of page level CSS came out of four pages, all of it quietly re-imposing the old pills over the top of the stylesheet.

The part worth keeping is the part that went wrong. A fix for two unstyled buttons shipped, and stayed invisible through a whole push cycle, because every page still asked for version six of a stylesheet that had become version seven. The rule was live and nothing was reading it. Looking a second time is the only reason it was caught.

entries.title: Twenty six dragons drawn blind, and the loop that fixed the drawing
entries.body:
Twenty six dragon initials got drawn for the entry pages, and the first set was not realistic in any way. That was the verdict and it was correct.

On paper the build was sound. A head, a tail, a wing and a spine spike drawn once each, then placed by transform onto every letter's own skeleton, so all twenty six would be the same animal rather than twenty six different ones. Consistent by construction. Ugly in fact.

The cause was not the geometry. Vector path data was going out blind, with nothing between emitting a coordinate and knowing what had appeared. Rendering the drawing to an image and looking at it closed that gap, and one pass afterwards did more than an hour of argument before it.

Looking settled something else that no description could. A tapered body makes a convincing serpent and an illegible letter. The S thinned to a whip and stopped being an S at all. Closed curves like C and O survived it, because a closed curve tolerates a thin tail. That conflict between the animal and the alphabet is obvious in one glance and invisible in a paragraph.

The European attempt read as a plesiosaur standing in a palm tree, and the whole line of work is dropped. A drawing process that cannot see its own output is not a drawing process. It is guessing with extra steps.

entries.title: Four sticks, a broken allocation table, and a success marker I wrote myself
entries.body:
The image of the failing stick refuses to mount. Corrupt and unreadable, according to Windows, which is the same fault that made the files unreadable on the stick in the first place.

So the filesystem got read by hand. A parser walks the boot sector, the directory tree and the cluster chains straight out of the raw image without asking the operating system for anything, and that part worked. Twenty two files, 11.04 gigabytes, every one of the five tracks listed by name and by size.

Then it failed at the only part that mattered. Following the chains produced 2,368 clusters where 69,296 were needed. Five files landed at roughly 30 megabytes apiece instead of 2,166, and their headers report 25,971 channels at 1.68 gigahertz, which is not audio. That is a parser running off the end of a broken chain and reading whatever sits behind it. The directory entries survived. The allocation table did not.

And the script announced RESULT: FILES RECOVERED, because it counted files written rather than files that turned out to be audio. That is the unconditional success marker the runner lint exists to catch, written again, by the same hand that wrote the lint. It took reading the header fields to notice, which is the only reason it was caught at all.

The count was wrong too. Four sticks, not two, and the twenty ninth of January turns out to exist on a second one with its own mixdown beside it. The broken stick is probably not the only copy of anything, which is the first good news this recovery has produced.

entries.title: Hemingway, Shelley and Dumas take equal part in the voice
entries.body:
Three writers now share the formula, and they cannot be blended, because at the level of a sentence they want opposite things. Hemingway takes out, Shelley puts in, Dumas keeps moving. Averaged evenly they make mush. So each one owns a different layer and all three are present in everything.

Hemingway owns the sentence. Concrete nouns, physical verbs, almost no adverbs, and the emotion put in an object rather than named. His iceberg comes with a leash on it here: omit only what was actually measured, because leaving out what nobody checked is a hole with confidence poured over it.

Shelley owns the frame. Every piece is testimony passed hand to hand, so say whose hand it came through. A measurement has a measurer, a log has the script that wrote it, a retraction has whoever got it wrong. Leave a mechanism dark when the dark is honest. Her moral was already the rule here: the crime is not making the thing, it is abandoning it and refusing to look at what it became.

Dumas owns the movement. Incident, reversal, a section that lands or hooks, and the one contract that outranks tidiness. The reader is never bored.

The measured counts still win. Shelley wrote in semicolons and there are none in the corpus, so the ban stands and she buys no exemption. The file itself then got cut to a third of its length, because less was always more here and it had stopped practising what it preached.

entries.title: One session of twenty five, and a stick that reads at one megabyte a second
entries.body:
Consent came through on the sixth, so the table recordings can be transcribed and quoted. The first one is done. 2021-01-26, two takes, 148.4 minutes, 19,426 words across five microphones. One session of twenty five.

The second stick is the problem, and most of what I said about it was wrong. Two imaging attempts died on their own timeouts, and the report was that the imager was grinding through 170,000 retries on damaged flash. The progress file from the second attempt says otherwise. 157 progress lines, zero bad blocks, every single read succeeded, throughput between 0.7 and 1.3 megabytes a second. Nothing was retrying. The device is about fifty times slower than a healthy stick and the scripts were fine.

The five WAV files fail at file level with error 1392 while every sector underneath them reads clean at raw level. That means the filesystem index is broken rather than the data, and the audio is very likely still there to be carved out by its own header once the image finishes. The imager now resumes from the 4.1 gigabytes already read and runs detached, so a timeout stops being fatal.

When a long job produces no output, the first thing to suspect is that it is slow. Not that it is broken. The way to tell them apart is a progress line, and the first imager did not write one, which is why an opinion got written up as a finding.

entries.title: Three things went wrong in one morning and none of them needed a person
entries.body:
Twice in one morning I asked Mac to restart the runner by hand. Line 41 of the runner says any file named cancel dropped into the control folder kills the running script. It has said that the whole time. Nobody needed to be asked anything.

Then an untested imager went straight at 14.6 gigabytes of unknown flash and retried at 64 kilobyte granularity on first contact. It ran 84 minutes, produced nothing, and buffered its log to the end, so killing it would have destroyed the only record of what it had learned. The rule that came out of that: sweep in large blocks, skip damage whole, map it, and go back for the fine work in a second pass.

Then a copy script wrote COPY-VERIFIED at the top of the folder and claimed success on a copy that had moved none of the five files it existed to protect. A success marker written unconditionally is not a check. It is a sticker.

All three landed on the one job that could not be retried, which is the shape of it. Work with no second attempt creates urgency, and urgency argues for speed at exactly the moment care is worth the most. The fixes are in code rather than in good intentions. The runner lint now warns on a long job with no incremental output and on a top level success marker, with five tests behind it, and the machine notes carry the cancel.

entries.title: Three finished products opened up, and all three were wrong somewhere
entries.body:
All three had passing test suites. All three were wrong in ways a test suite was never going to see, and the way they were found was running each one as the person who would use it.

CampaignOS claimed in its own register entry that it refuses an ambiguous target rather than guessing which goblin you meant. It did not. Four goblins on the board, say kill goblin, and the damage landed on Goblin 1. Goblin 2 takes 2 was not understood at all. The back button panicked on an imported index and initiative was a label rather than an order. Fixed and pinned in place, then a ten round fight on real stat blocks saved and reloaded identical. 52 tests.

DM Toolbox had a rules tier marked RAW, meaning the rule as written, and 8 of its 13 entries were paraphrase with a page number attached to lend it weight. Separately the Faction Web wrote a full campaign backup every 4.1 seconds while sitting idle doing nothing. Seven every thirty seconds. Now none. All 30 rules are verbatim now, with a test that checks them against the source text rather than against somebody's memory of it.

AxiomTEA is the one that is finished. The built binary misread three real public documents: relative percentages taken as efficiencies, a chemistry attributed from anywhere in the document rather than from the claim, and utilisation ratios read as efficiencies. It also reported its own bundled dependencies as unknown, which is the exact failure the health endpoint was built to catch. 26 new tests, 297 passing, rebuilt, and the verdicts come out right. Two rocket ceilings disagreed with the project's own provenance file and the file won.

A green suite means the code does what the tests say. It has nothing to say about whether the tests asked for the right thing.

entries.title: Seven models had been switched off for two days and no round said so
entries.body:
A script on the fourth set seven browser models to disabled with a note attached saying temporary, for one API only round. It was never reverted. Every panel after that ran on seven seats instead of fourteen, including the two attack rounds and the whole final pass, and not one of them mentioned it.

Restored, with the old config kept. Speed is a flag now rather than an edit: one switch drops the browsers for a single round and puts them back afterwards, and the roster refuses to stay quiet about a temporary marker that has outlived its round.

The bigger finding underneath it. Seventeen live seats turned out to be eleven distinct families. Google held four of them, one pinning no model at all. Two more seats were serving the same Llama from different companies. A quorum built like that counts the same voice several times and calls the agreement consensus, which is the exact failure a quorum exists to catch. A round now removes duplicates by model, then by credential, then by family, and the surplus seats wait as first refusal backfill rather than being thrown away. The coding agents came off the panel entirely. They are bridges, and a bridge is not a witness.

And the one that cost something. Google puts the API key in the query string. A 503 raised an error carrying the whole URL, so the key was printed, written to an output file, stored in two working folders, mirrored to Drive, and committed. It sat in the open for five days. Every path that handled a key on purpose kept the rule. The path that handled an error had never been asked to.

Scrubbing lives inside the error object now, so every future raise site is covered without anyone remembering to cover it. That fixes the next one. It does not fix this one, because redaction does not un leak what already leaked, and the key still has to be rotated by a person.

entries.title: Fourteen projects off the disk, and all fourteen still on the site
entries.body:
Fourteen projects came off the disk today and stayed on the site. That is the whole shape of it. The files are gone and the record is not.

They stopped because free tools already do the job and do it better. EpiGuide against CHOPCHOP and CRISPOR, which search a whole genome where it counted repeats inside one submitted sequence. CrystalGen against pymatgen and the Materials Project, which is a database this never had. SynapseGraph against GROBID, open since 2011, scoring about 0.87 across ninety thousand references, where this one matched a single paper. NeuroSteer against TransformerLens and nnsight, which steer real models rather than a toy transformer trained on nothing. AegisBox against gVisor and nsjail, which do at the kernel what it attempted inside one Python interpreter. AxiomVerify against Lean and Coq. SovereignVault against age and libsodium, in the exact application where an audited primitive earns its dependency. Kinematix against PyBullet and MuJoCo, which already implement the three papers it was finally checked against. Four more went with them for reasons of their own.

Every one has a teardown here now, and every register card keeps its status, its reason, and the name of what to use instead. None of it is hidden. A record that does not survive the thing it records was never a record.

Nothing was deleted. Twenty eight directories moved into a trash folder that writes down where each came from, and a restore takes a substring. The removal is one commit in a repo with no remote, so the history still holds every file.

The removal broke in two ways before it worked, and both are written down. Passing an array of paths to a PowerShell script through -File flattens it, so the first attempt moved nothing while reporting no fault. That same run then staged two uncommitted edits it had not authored and committed them, which is the one thing the rule about external edits exists to prevent. The commit was reset, those two files were given their own checkpoint untouched, and the second run did the work.

entries.title: The rules were arriving at 44 percent and nothing said so
entries.body:
The standing rules that govern every session were being delivered at 44.3 percent, and nothing anywhere said so. There was no measurement at all. That number exists because building the measurement was the first thing the rebuild did.

Two faults underneath it. A script joined the AmoebiX status line and an 8,784 character store of rules into a 4,000 character budget by keeping the first 4,000 characters and dropping the rest, so the newest rules were the half thrown away. And a hook that fires after a compaction had been registered and firing for eleven days while delivering nothing: its continuity file had never existed, half of it was gated on a variable nobody sets, its one instruction named a command that was not registered, and it wrote to plain output when the channel only reads one specific field. Four faults in a single hook, and it never reported a problem because it never reported anything. What actually carried context across a compaction that whole time was Claude Code's own summary.

The rebuild itself. Twenty three hooks across seven events down to five across four. Twenty four hook files down to five. Nineteen backups of one settings file down to none. Nineteen stale skills on disk down to seven, one of them still naming a system that no longer exists and pointing at a runner path that moved. Twenty eight rules at 44.3 percent became thirty at 100, reported on both channels at the start of every session.

The part worth keeping is that the check was made to fail. Overfilling the brief past its budget produces the word TRUNCATED rather than a quiet cut. Removing the brief entirely produces an announcement that delivery is zero and the session should be treated as ungoverned. A check that has never failed has not been tested, and a check that cannot fail is decoration.

Nothing was deleted. Fourteen items sit in a trash folder with their origin paths recorded and a restore command that takes a substring, and the rollback was rehearsed against the real archive before any of it was believed.

One thing got settled by reading rather than building. AmoebiX was going to become an MCP server, on the reasoning that a tool survives a compaction while an instruction does not. The reasoning holds. The mechanism does not: Cowork does not run local MCP servers, it was reported and closed as not planned, and the registration has been sitting there invisible the whole time. The remote version was declined rather than offered as normal, because it would turn a local toolbox that runs tasks, reads files and holds provider keys into an execution service facing the internet.

AmoebiX itself got three fixes. Its budget flag was applied by slicing the model list before dispatch, which walked straight past both the cooldown filter and the scoreboard. A budget is a seat count, not a guest list. The thread pool joined before the browser loop began, so a round cost the slowest API call plus every browser call added together, with the slow chain scheduled last; the browsers start first on their own thread now and run alongside the rest. And a model that failed lost its seat for the whole round, so one bounded pass backfills it. Three live rounds after the change: one answer out of three, then two, then three answered and none failed.

CampaignOS closed at 1.0 in the small hours. Twenty five tests, the condition grid collapsed into pills that read back what is actually applied, a manual, an architecture document, and a build that produces the exe, the msi and the setup installer.

entries.title: A fight tracker finished, and two modules killed for already existing
entries.body:
CampaignOS was further along than its own register entry said. It builds, 25 tests pass, and it produces an installer. What it did not have was a single design document: the two that carried the original plan were deprecated at the end of August and deleted, and the file left behind was one line long.

The interesting hole was in the tests. Fourteen were passing, covering the parser, undo and redo, and JSON round-trips. None of them checked that damage reaches the right creature, because every mutation lived inside a Tauri command that a test cannot call. Inverting the damage arm from minus to plus left all fourteen green. So did deleting the cap on healing. The pure half is now split out and tested, and the same two mutations fail nine tests between them.

Two modules got killed rather than built. The Vault and The Arbiter were scoped for the next version, and both already exist in DM Toolbox, down to the same treasure tiers and the same three levels of rules strictness. Building them again would have turned a fight tracker into a second toolbox and spent the fast start it was told to protect.

The best thing in the app was already there. Two goblins on the board and a DM who says only goblin gets a refusal and a list of which ones were meant. It will not pick one. Damage landing on a creature nobody named is the failure you would not notice until someone died wrong.

entries.title: DM Toolbox builds into an exe that actually opens
entries.body:
Eight modules had been written and never once packaged. The README said so plainly: built and smoke-tested under Linux, never run on a real Windows machine, and that was the one thing the environment could not check. It can now, so it did.

The build failed first time, and the reason is worth keeping. Bare python, pip and pyinstaller pointed at three different places on the same machine. python resolved to an unrelated tool's virtualenv with no pywebview in it, pip resolved to a completely different interpreter, and pyinstaller was not a command at all. So the install step exited zero and reported success while the interpreter that would actually run the app still could not import the thing that had just been installed. Both launchers now pick one interpreter up front and bind every step to it, and the build proves the install landed there rather than trusting an exit code.

Second time it built. Twenty megabytes, one file, and it opens a real window with all eight modules in it and writes saves that survive a relaunch.

One more trap on the way, recorded because it nearly got written up as a failure. Asking Windows for the process's main window returns nothing at all on a working build, because a one-file package runs a small parent that launches the real program, and the window belongs to the child. Ask the parent and you get told there is no window. The app was on screen the whole time.

entries.title: Ran the programs instead of the tests
entries.body:
Every project in the set has a passing test suite and nobody had ever asked whether the answers were right. So the programs got run instead.

AegisBox claims network blocking, memory caps, watchdog timeouts and filesystem protection, and its ten tests never once try to break out of any of them. Real attacks say the watchdog holds and the airgap holds. Filesystem confinement was wide open and is now closed. The memory cap still fails on Windows, because the fix there is a job object nobody has written yet. And the threat scanner ships with detection on and blocking off, so the default path rates code CRITICAL_THREAT and then runs it. That looks like a security control and behaves like a logger.

OmniFleet served exactly one ride per vehicle out of two hundred submitted, then stopped. There was no time loop, so no car ever finished a trip and picked up a second passenger, and the fleet sizing sweep the whole project is named for could not mean anything. That one got fixed before the day ended. Dispatch now carries a clock per vehicle and measures the wait from the request to the pickup, which is the number a rider actually feels.

CrystalGen returned negative zero for table salt, because neither sodium nor chlorine was in its element table and it quietly skipped whatever it did not recognise. Table now holds fifty one elements with cited sources. The fix exposed the real defect underneath: the valence field was never read at all, so magnesium oxide and table salt landed within a tenth of an electron volt of each other despite four times the lattice energy. Adding the charge product cut mean error by a third.

The part worth keeping is the retractions. Three times in one day a confident defect got written up in somebody else's code and the fault was in the measurement. Read the x component of a population vector against an angle in radians and a working neural decoder looks like a coin toss. Score ranking on seven compounds and 74.5 percent looks like 57. Compare extraction against reference counts that were invented rather than counted and correct output looks like overcounting.

When the measurement says the code is badly broken, check the measurement first. Re-measuring is cheaper than rewriting, and a confident negative claim about someone's work should cost more scrutiny than a positive one, not less. The retractions stay in the findings file rather than getting deleted. A record that tidies away its own mistakes is worth nothing.

entries.title: The site becomes a record instead of a magazine
entries.body:
Rebuilt the site around what actually happens here. Three reading rooms stay for finished writing. Four working rooms added: this log, a project register, the map of the future, and the quorum record. Governance amended to match, since it named exactly three rooms and now names seven.

The register lists every project, started or not. Twenty seven of them, five working, sixteen still a README and a stub. Presenting the unstarted ones as unstarted is the point.

Also today: two teardowns published, AxiomTEA and Dungeon Cue. A voice-checking pipeline built, calibrated, and halted on purpose. The site repo moved off Google Drive, where a syncing folder had been quietly rewriting a live git directory.

entries.title: A machine that measured my own writing, and why it was switched off
entries.body:
Built four gates to check whether a draft sounds like me. A free regex pass on banned words, a local embedding score against a corpus of my own writing, an LLM comparator, a fact pass. Got the first two working and calibrated the threshold to zero false rejections across thirty one samples.

Then halted it. Its main output was a list of fixes, and I do not revise. I write once and abandon what does not work, so the tool's primary product had no consumer. The regex check stays because it costs nothing and already caught a real defect in itself: the banned word list would have vetoed a poem I wrote in 2016.

The rest is archived with a written condition for waking it up.

entries.title: Draega canon pulled off World Anvil, and one published entry found to be wrong
entries.body:
Mirrored thirty two World Anvil articles into the repo. All of it mine, no AI anywhere in it, which makes it the clean counterweight to a worldbuilding compendium that got partly AI-filled and has been flagged untrusted since.

The pull turned up an error in a live entry. A 2020 site I built myself puts Anjax in the four-person player party. The published piece files him among the captains and generals. The published piece is wrong, and it is wrong in exactly the way a contaminated source predicts: smooth, confident, and traceable to nothing.

entries.title: The heaviest week. AxiomTEA, AmoebiX, and the bridge
entries.body:
Five hundred and fifty four documents in seven days, the largest stretch of work in the record.

AxiomTEA took a hundred and eighty two of them and came out the other side as a shipping product. AmoebiX took a hundred and twenty and became the thing I now use every day. The agent bridge took seventy nine. The Golden Sea campaign took fifty eight and reached twenty four modules.

The Windows runner was built this week too, which is why a session in the cloud can now do things on this machine without me pasting commands into a terminal.

entries.title: Fifteen projects fall out of the research
entries.body:
The Moonshots corpus turned into a taxonomy and then into a portfolio. Twenty four branches, fifteen projects, each with a code and a branch and a capital figure of zero.

Most of them are scaffolds and the README says so now, though it did not at first. It claimed fifty of fifty tests passing and pointed at a test runner that does not exist. That got corrected rather than quietly deleted, because a repo overstating its own state is the same failure the flagship project exists to detect in other people's claims.

AxiomTEA is the one that got real.

entries.title: Two large questions with no product attached
entries.body:
Asked how you would redesign civilization if you could. The answer refused the framing: do not try to fix people, redesign the incentive architecture, because civilization is extraordinarily good at local optimization and extraordinarily bad at global.

The next day, asked for the ten most consequential bets humanity has made since 2021, chosen on real capital and real hardware rather than noise, and stacked rather than listed.

entries.title: Fable Archive, and three tools at once
entries.body:
Two hundred and thirty four documents. The Fable Archive alone accounts for a hundred and sixty five of them.

Dungeon Cue, DMToolbox, SoundCue and MudBuddy all moved in the same week, which is either productive or a diagnosis depending on who is counting.

entries.title: Dungeon Cue starts
entries.body:
The mouse is on the wrong side of the table. That is the whole problem statement, and Dungeon Cue is the answer to it: say the phrase, the rain starts, nobody looks up.

SoundCue moved the same week, and its electric blue and gold became the visual language for everything after.

entries.title: The workspace itself
entries.body: Fifty documents, most of them the working environment rather than any product. This is where the record starts. Before this week the folders hold invoices, resumes, a dissertation, and descriptions written for text games, and nothing that became any of this.
